articles.title: ‘Couldn’t wait to kill Indians’: US teen’s neo-Nazi manifesto reveals Hindu temple attack plot
articles.summary: A 19-year-old US man who allegedly told co-workers he “couldn’t wait to kill Indian people” was arrested over a suspected mass shooting plot targeting a
articles.body: A 19-year-old US man who allegedly told co-workers he “couldn’t wait to kill Indian people” was arrested over a suspected mass shooting plot targeting a Hindu temple in Aurora, near Chicago. Police say he had shared a racist manifesto and visited the temple on the day investigators believe he planned to attack.Alexandros Paporakis, a Taco Bell cashier from Palatine, Illinois, faces felony charges of making a terrorist threat and unlawfully possessing a rifle with a barrel shorter than 16 inches. A judge ordered him detained before trial on Wednesday. His next court appearance is scheduled for October 30.According to prosecutors, Paporakis openly identified himself as a white supremacist at work and regularly made disparaging remarks about people of different races, including Indians. His colleagues told investigators that he discussed Nazis and violence and that his behaviour had intensified in the days before his arrest.On Saturday, he allegedly told a co-worker that he “couldn’t wait to kill Indian people” and spoke about a plan involving a Hindu temple in Aurora, a city about 65 kilometres southwest of Palatine. He also told a colleague that Sunday would be “a special day”, according to court documents.Planning attack for 2 yearsProsecutors allege that Paporakis had been planning an attack for about two years, narrowing his focus to a specific location in recent months. He allegedly researched the target using YouTube and Google Street View.Investigators say the material he shared with a co-worker included an eight-page document titled Why I Fought: A.K.A. (Aurora Shooter’s Manifesto). According to a court document obtained by the Associated Press, the manifesto described Indian, Jewish and Black people as “subhumans” and outlined a plan to kill as many of them as possible.In the document, Paporakis allegedly described himself as a “sociopathic white supremacist Neo Nazi filled with hatred, fantasising about mass murder nearly every day”. He also portrayed his outward identity as a working college student as a facade concealing his violent intentions, according to the documents.Gun allegedly jammed during visit to templePolice believe Paporakis may have attempted to carry out the attack on Sunday, October 11. Surveillance footage showed his car entering the parking lot of a large Hindu temple in Aurora at around 12.25 pm and leaving approximately 13 minutes later. Investigators said he appeared to be alone in the vehicle.The precise intended target has not been officially identified by police and remains under investigation. The Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora subsequently alerted its members to a security threat, according to The New York Times.Prosecutors allege that Paporakis contacted a co-worker later that day and said his gun had jammed. He reportedly said he had left the scene “super fast” without being seen. He also allegedly sent the colleague a video showing the rifle failing to fire and said he wanted to repair it and try again.According to court documents, he told the co-worker that the man he had fired at had been “certainly saved by his God today”. The documents do not establish the identity of the person he allegedly fired at or provide further details about the circumstances.The co-worker contacted police, prompting officers from Palatine and neighbouring Mount Prospect to locate Paporakis. Investigators believed he might attempt to carry out the plan again, and officers arrested him outside his home on Sunday afternoon.Rifle, ammunition and Nazi imagery recoveredA search of Paporakis’ home uncovered an AR-style rifle without a serial number, loaded magazines, hundreds of rounds of ammunition and tactical equipment, police and prosecutors said. Investigators also recovered a tactical vest with body armour, items bearing Nazi symbolism and a gas canister labelled with an anti-South Asian slur.The evidence, along with the alleged manifesto and electronic communications, is being examined as part of the investigation. The FBI’s Chicago Field Office assisted local police in reviewing the material.“The seriousness of this alleged threat cannot be overstated,” Palatine Police Chief William Nord said, describing the protection of places of worship as a law enforcement priority.Ryan Whalen, the FBI’s Chicago special agent in charge, said the agency worked with local and state authorities to identify and investigate threats driven by extremist ideologies. He credited the rapid response by the Palatine and Mount Prospect police departments with ensuring that the suspect was taken into custody without harm to the community.Paporakis has been charged with making a terrorist threat, a Class X felony, and unlawful possession of a rifle with a barrel shorter than 16 inches, a Class 3 felony. It was not immediately clear whether he had entered a plea or secured legal representation.Arrest renews concern over anti-Indian hateThe case has intensified concerns about hostility towards Indian Americans and other South Asian communities in the United States, particularly as anti-immigration rhetoric and disputes over skilled-worker visas have become increasingly contentious.The FBI does not record crimes against Indian Americans as a separate category. Data on anti-Hindu and anti-Sikh offences therefore offer only a partial picture of the hostility faced by communities whose members often trace their roots to India.Physical attacks and vandalism have also affected Hindu places of worship. In June 2025, between 20 and 30 rounds were reportedly fired at a Krishna temple in Spanish Fork, Utah, while people were inside; no injuries were reported. A separate temple in Santa Clara, California, was vandalised later that summer.Online hostility has been more pronounced. A report by the Centre for the Study of Organised Hate found that the monthly volume of hateful posts about South Asians on X more than tripled between January 2024 and June 2026.Researchers have linked some of the hostility to disputes over immigration and the H-1B visa programme, which US employers use to hire skilled foreign workers. Indians receive more than 70% of H-1B visas.The ministry of external affairs also said it was “deeply concerned” by the alleged plot, describing its reported anti-Hindu and racist nature as “particularly disturbing”. Official spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal called for a thorough investigation, accountability for those responsible and measures to ensure the safety of the Indian community in the US.You use AI every day. articles.title: Philippines: 'Onion cartel' fined $28m for 2022 price crisis
articles.summary: Onions were worth more than the daily minimum wage at the height of the price surge in 2022.
articles.body:
Filipino authorities say they have fined six companies 1.76 billion pesos ($27.9m; £21m) for forming an "onion cartel" that caused the price of the vegetable to skyrocket.

In 2022 the price of onions, a staple of Philippine kitchens, surged to a record 800 pesos per 1kg, surpassing the country's daily minimum wage and overtaking the price of meat.

The crisis put pressure on then newly-elected President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, who had promised to bring down surging food prices.

The Philippine Competition Commission (PCC) said Wednesday the fine against the companies, comprised of onion importers and storage and shipping firms, was the largest since its formation in 2016.

For months between late 2022 to early 2023, onions disappeared from restaurant menus and became the object of smuggling attempts.

The bulbous vegetable even became something of a status symbol, having been used on at least one occasion as a wedding bouquet.

Authorities approved the emergency import of onions and Marcos vowed to go after those behind the shortage, saying there were "Filipinos dying from starvation and poverty because of what they are doing".

The crisis ended as local bumper harvests entered the market later in 2023 and prices stabilised.

A parliamentary committee tasked to investigate the price crisis said a cartel was behind the "artificial" surge in onion prices.

The PCC said evidence retrieved during raids on the companies showed that the six firms had collectively controlled nearly 50% of all approved import clearances for onions in 2020 and 2021.

The companies were involved in an "illegal market allocation scheme in the importation, cold storage, and whole sale distribution", the commission said.

The hefty fine shows a "commitment to holding cartels accountable across all sectors of the economy and protecting consumers from the harmful effects of anti-competitive conduct", the PCC said.

The commission also said that offenders may also be criminally prosecuted by the Department of Justice.

articles.title: Watch: Elon Musk's 'flying Tesla' takes off, flips mid-air and lands safely in demo
articles.summary: Tesla has unveiled a redesigned version of its next-generation Roadster electric sports car, featuring built-in thrusters and flying-car-like manoeuvres,
articles.body: Tesla has unveiled a redesigned version of its next-generation Roadster electric sports car, featuring built-in thrusters and flying-car-like manoeuvres, nearly nine years after first presenting the prototype. The company said production of the two-seater vehicle would begin in 2028.The demonstration, held at a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, on Thursday, showed the vehicle driving upside down on a ramp using a suction system, turning in mid-air and landing with the help of built-in thrusters. The Roadster has been developed in collaboration with Elon Musk's rocket company, SpaceX.The legality and practical use of these features on public roads remained unclear.Musk said the Roadster could accelerate from zero to 60 miles per hour in less than one second and achieve a top speed exceeding 230 mph.Tesla Roadster's long-awaited returnTesla first unveiled a prototype of the second-generation Roadster in 2017, promising deliveries in 2020. The latest announcement pushes the expected production timeline to 2028, extending the wait for the electric sports car by several years.Musk had previously said the four-seat Roadster would offer a range of 620 miles (1,000 km) on a single charge.Despite its ambitious performance targets, Musk has played down the vehicle's potential contribution to Tesla's finances. In 2023, he described the project as a "small potato situation" that would not "move the needle in a major way financially."However, analysts see the Roadster as an opportunity for Tesla to showcase its engineering capabilities and strengthen its premium brand image."Tesla does not currently have a halo car, or high-performance luxury vehicle designed to showcase an automaker's best engineering and technology. The Roadster will be Tesla's new halo car," Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein said in a note last month.Goldstein expects Tesla to sell around 2,000 Roadsters annually, a small fraction of the 1.6 million vehicles the company sold last year.From electric sports cars to AI and roboticsThe original Roadster, launched in 2008 and sold until 2012, was Tesla's first electric vehicle. Built on a Lotus Elise chassis, it helped challenge perceptions about the performance capabilities of electric cars.Tesla subsequently expanded its lineup with the Model S and Model 3 sedans and the Model X and Model Y SUVs.The latest Roadster reveal comes as the company increasingly shifts its focus towards artificial intelligence, autonomous driving and robotics, alongside its traditional electric vehicle business.This year, Tesla stopped selling the Model S and Model X to free up production capacity for its Optimus humanoid robots. The company has also introduced the Cybercab, a two-seat robotaxi designed without conventional manual driving controls.The Roadster's return therefore comes at a time when Tesla is seeking to demonstrate its technological ambitions beyond conventional electric vehicles.You use AI every day. articles.title: They fled Russia, but the West sent them back
articles.summary: Over the past year there has been a stark rise in anti-government activists deported to Russia from the EU and US where they were seeking refuge.
articles.body:
Russian security services were waiting when the flight landed in Moscow in December. On board were Russians the US had deported, including activists denied political asylum.

"It was unbelievably frightening. My knees were shaking with fear," says Katya, one of the deportees. We have changed her name to protect her identity, as she remains in Russia.

Katya had left Russia and claimed asylum in the US two years earlier.

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, many countries publicly welcomed fleeing Russians. But more than four years later, attitudes have hardened. The numbers of anti-war Russians forcibly returned from Western countries is rising, and Katya's experience highlights the potential risks they face.

US authorities rejected her application for asylum, after she said she had provided evidence that she had taken part in protests and was a member of an opposition movement.

In Moscow, Katya says officers from the FSB security service handed all the male deportees military papers, requiring them to register with the local enlistment office, from where men are often sent to the war in Ukraine. Another passenger on the flight and an activist confirmed her account.

The officers interrogated her, and many others, for several hours.

"At one point, they found incriminating information on my phone," says Katya, "Their faces changed in a second. I was very afraid that they would simply bundle me off somewhere."

Katya was eventually released and allowed to stay with relatives. But she says police continue to call her and visit her at home.

"I feel as if I'm in a cage, like in a zoo," she says, "Whenever I see a police car, I feel terrified and start thinking, "What if they're coming for me?"

Katya showed the BBC documents and photographs confirming her story, which matches accounts from other deportees.

Removals from the US rose from 222 in 2023 to more than 1,200 in 2025, amid a wider increase in deportations under President Donald Trump's second term. Activists say Russian deportees included dissidents and Russian army deserters, some of whom were imprisoned or sent to war after returning to Russia.

One such case is Leonid Melekhin, an anti-war activist who sought asylum in the US after being arrested at protests in Russia. He had posted photographs of Russian President Vladimir Putin online with the message "Putin: murderer, fascist, usurper". After being deported back home last year, Melekhin was charged with "justifying terrorism" and sentenced to six years in prison.

"We have several examples of people who got eight years in prison when they crossed the [Russian] border," says Andrei Pivovarov, from Russia's exiled opposition Anti-War Committee.

And deportations are taking place from Europe too. His organisation has changed its advice to dissidents escaping Russia: the EU is no longer safe, it is better to seek refuge elsewhere.

Germany has sharply increased the number of Russian nationals it deports. Seven were sent back in 2023, rising to more than 110 in 2025, according to German government figures. More than 21,000 Russians sought asylum in Germany between 2022 and 2025, but the proportion of positive decisions fell from 29% in 2023 to just 6.8% in the first eleven months of 2025.

"Protection is only granted if there is an actual, well-founded fear of persecution," Germany's migration and asylum agency, BAMF, told the BBC.

Last year, Berlin suspended its humanitarian visa programme for Russians, and across the EU, the proportion of Russian applicants granted some form of asylum protection fell from 23% in 2024 to around 17% in the first nine months of 2025, according to EU data.

Russian opposition activists fleeing repression have become caught up in a wider crackdown on immigration, as governments across Europe and the US toughen rules amid political pressure over high numbers of irregular migrants and asylum applications, as well as over security concerns.

Western governments are "focused on limiting humanitarian programmes and asylum seekers", says lawyer Anastasia Burakova, founder of rights group Kovcheg (Ark), which helps anti-war Russians leave the country. The clampdown is "in response to public concerns and rising support for right-wing populist parties", she adds.

Following a negative asylum decision, Russian nationals are often given the chance to leave independently, but a rising number are being forcibly returned to Russia, usually escorted via third countries.

Several Russian activists in exile told the BBC that immigration officials had told them they faced "no danger" in Russia, and that officials often lacked an adequate understanding of the risks that activists face.

"I tried to explain that if they sent me back, I would be put in prison, or sent to war where I'd be killed," explains former soldier Artyom, who deserted from the Russian Army in 2022 after officers threatened to send him to Ukraine. "They just didn't believe me."

He says he provided US authorities with proof that a criminal investigation had been opened against him back in Russia for desertion. But he was put on a deportation flight back to Moscow via Egypt.

"I was preparing for death," says the former soldier, "I was thinking, 'how can I die without it being painful?'".

Back in Moscow, Artyom was held in a military detention facility but managed to escape. He is now in hiding abroad.

"Another country could investigate me better and give me asylum. Why didn't they give me that chance? Instead they deported me specifically to Russia," says the deserter. "It ruined my life."

The US Department of Homeland Security told the BBC: "All illegal aliens receive due process. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them."

The asylum clampdown comes as repression inside Russia has reached "an unprecedented level", according to Nobel Prize-winning Russian human rights group Memorial. Their list of political prisoners grew from 803 to 1,265 during 2025, a record increase.

The Russian Embassy in London did not respond to a request for comment.

Anti-war activist Mikhail says he and his wife Dasha are awaiting deportation from Finland "any day". Their names have been changed to protect their identity, as Mikhail fears for relatives back home.

Russian authorities blocked his social media accounts over anti-war posts, and police visited his mother and accused him of spreading "fake information".

Dasha is a Jehovah's Witness, an organisation banned as "extremist" in Russia. The couple provided Finnish authorities with evidence, seen by the BBC, including a video of Russian police telling his mother that more than 300 posts had violated Russian law. A single post can result in a long prison sentence.

The Finnish Immigration Service has rejected their asylum request five times, deciding there is "no reasonable basis to believe" the couple would face serious rights violations if returned.

"We're sitting here and someone could knock on our door at any moment, take us to the Russian border and simply hand us over to Russian officers," says Mikhail. "We fear for our lives!"

"We came to Finland for help, and they're refusing us," he adds. "My wife cries constantly."

Amnesty International, which is supporting the couple, says they could face a "real risk" of detention, prosecution, imprisonment and torture if returned.

The Finnish Immigration Service said all asylum decisions were based on international refugee law standards, and the share of Russian citizens receiving asylum was in line with EU averages.

For Mikhail and Dasha, the threat of deportation comes as more Russians may be considering leaving.

There are rumours that Vladimir Putin may announce a new wave of mobilisation to boost the ranks of his army in Ukraine, which the Kremlin denies. The last mobilisation in 2022 prompted hundreds of thousands of Russians to flee, many to ex-Soviet states such as Armenia and Georgia.

Anastasia Burakova's organisation says requests for help from Russians wanting to leave rose tenfold in August compared with May. For those now looking to escape, the question is whether the West will offer them refuge — or send them back.

articles.title: Met needs to move away from criminalising sex workers, officers say after Levy failings
articles.summary: The force is piloting a two-officer female team in north London to engage with street sex workers, in a bid to improve trust.
articles.body:
The Met need to move away from criminalising women involved in street sex work in the wake of the Simon Levy case, officers have told the BBC.

Levy, a convicted sex offender, was left to kill two women and rape another - all of whom were vulnerable and sometimes engaged in street sex work - due to a series of failings, including by the force.

Now the Met is piloting a new two-officer female team in north London to engage with street sex workers, in a bid to improve trust and encourage them to report crimes committed against them.

The Levy case exposed grave failings in policing and also the inherent tension in its approach to street sex workers.

How police let a registered sex offender murder and attack women

Serial sex offender guilty of double murder and rape

Sex work is legal in the UK, excluding Northern Ireland, but related activities like soliciting for clients in public places - known as street sex work - working together, or brothel keeping, pimping and advertising sexual services are all illegal.

Street sex workers are also often targeted by police using anti-social behaviour powers.

Many women who require protection naturally fear arrest and do not trust officers to investigate violence.

On patrol with officers who run new Met scheme

The BBC joined a patrol with the two plain-clothed female officers who run the new Met scheme, Operation Amicus.

They described hearing about endemic levels of male violence against the women they have met, who come from a cohort of 80 women in the area identified as involved in street-based sex work.

"Every single one has reported something," one of the officers said, "whether they've been raped, they've been punched - they've been attacked in some way, shape or form."

The officers, whom the BBC agreed not to name, said several women have been too scared to report abuse to the police.

The officers described encountering an appalling situation in which women are repeatedly attacked by men but think the police cannot be trusted to help.

Some women "expect to be raped and sexually assaulted by customers - it's just become the norm, so [they think] what is the point in reporting [it]", one of the officers said.

The new team added that they were trying to help the women to formally report crimes.

"Once they report one and they realise they're being listened to, they then start to report the next one because they know that somebody's [going] to turn up and somebody's going to listen and [they're] going to be taken seriously."

The officers the BBC spoke to said the Met needs to move away from criminalising women involved in street sex work – saying it's "not fair" when "they're just trying to survive".

They said they were also aware of concerns by residents about sex work in their streets and the need to tackle organised crime.

Levy, who was given a whole-life term in August, sexually assaulted women at random on London's public transport network, as well as elsewhere. He now has convictions for attacking 13 women he encountered on the Tube and trains, as well as at music events and even in prison.

He also targeted vulnerable women involved in street sex work.

He killed Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo in March 2025 and Sheryl Wilkins five months later.

Prior to their murders, Levy had raped a third woman, in January 2025. The rape survivor told police what had happened while she was being arrested by Met officers for allegedly breaching a community banning order.

But the Met didn't properly engage with her and eventually closed the rape case. It was only re-opened when Levy went on to murder Valencia-Trujillo and Wilkins, which took place in the same section of a car park where he had raped the surviving victim.

The survivor later said in a statement "nobody ever listened to me" and that the police who interviewed her had spoken to her "like a child".

The Met and the Crown Prosecution Service have apologised over a series of decisions that left Levy free to roam the streets.

Supt Rob Gibbs said the new team is "an acknowledgement that we needed to change the way in which we were working" and move away from criminalising sex work.

"Women get stuck in the criminal justice system" for minor offences, he said - and this leads to "more sex working and actually we need to break that cycle".

Gibbs added that women involved in street-based sex work were at the "most harsh end of violence against women and girls".

While on patrol, the BBC met a woman we are calling Alice to protect her identity.

She told us most women she knows who are homeless and engage in sex work in Tottenham, north London, have not reported assaults for fear of the police and being arrested themselves.

She said two men have attacked her in separate incidents this year, including a man who violently assaulted her after she declined to take his money and sell him sex a few months ago.

"I was scared to contact the police," she said. "When I went to the hospital I begged the doctors, 'please don't phone the police because I'll get arrested'."

Alice said she first met the Met's female sex-worker liaison team when she was attacked by another man after falling asleep in a lift to her mum's apartment.

"They came and said, 'look, we're not here to arrest you, get you in trouble, we're here to support you'," Alice said.

'Women describe absolute terror from the police'

The Met says the new team has already improved safeguarding and increased reports of rape and sexual offences, as well as improving information sharing to identify "the most dangerous perpetrators of violence against women and girls".

However, the English Collective of Prostitutes (ECP) - which advocates for decriminalisation of sex workers - said that previous police clear-up operations on organised crime in London and around the country have led to a longstanding history of police prioritising prosecuting sex workers, rather than investigating male violence against them.

Laura Watson, a caseworker for the ECP, said a "very intense and aggressive police crackdown" in north London had led to "quite aggressive arrests of women" in Enfield and Haringey.

"In some cases, closure zones and antisocial behaviour orders which banned women from entire areas in some cases" led to "mass criminalisation because women were breaching those orders".

She said "women really describe absolute terror from the police, running up and down the road, running away from the police".

Most street sex workers are "mothers working to feed themselves and their children", she told us.

Prof Kate Brown, from the University of York, whose research focuses on policing interventions with sex workers, said creating such teams was not in itself a solution.

"Our research shows that sex work liaison officers can make a real difference to safety and access to justice, but only when they are designed and delivered in the right way," she said.

Her research centre is working with 12 police forces out of 43 in England and Wales, to safely implement sex worker liaison teams.

But she said these teams "cannot fix a system that continues to police and criminalise sex workers" and that "decriminalisation is the best way to deliver safety and justice" for them.

The Met said that if the team was "successful in improving confidence within the community", then this approach would be "rolled out across the force".

A Home Office spokesperson said: "Our commitment to halving violence against women and girls within a decade includes tackling the serious exploitation and abuse associated with prostitution.

"We expect the police to treat all victims of offences with dignity, and every investigation to be conducted thoroughly. We also continue to work with NGOs and charities to ensure women and girls at risk of sexual exploitation are protected."

articles.title: The whole street was in flames: Inside the West Midlands wildfire disaster
articles.summary: Harrowing 999 calls and eyewitness accounts tell the story of a day authorities say must not reoccur.
articles.body:
It is 13:00 BST on the hottest day of the year and five engines are speeding towards a grass fire in Birmingham.

Temperatures are creeping towards 38C and it has been yet another busy morning at West Midlands Fire Control.

But within minutes, the switchboard is jammed with panicked calls about wildfires in fields and parks that are moving dangerously close to homes.

"We had 20-plus 999 calls in a queue," recalls control room firefighter Lauren Nightingale.

"It was busy, bordering on uncomfortable – and then extreme."

Intense heatwaves and weeks without rain have left the ground tinder dry and multiple fires have started simultaneously.

"Within 10 minutes, we were experiencing conditions that were well and truly out of the norm," Nightingale, aged 29, says.

Before the day is out, she and her colleagues will deal with almost 2,000 calls, more than triple the number taken on the same day the previous year.

Holly, 14, is home alone in Stourbridge playing Roblox on her iPad. She is still in her pyjamas – it is the summer holidays – and her curtains are shut.

Her mum and sister are 140 miles away with friends in Minehead and her mum's partner is at work. Holly is chatting on her mobile to a friend when the house alarm begins to blare.

Unsure what to do, she calls her mum, who tells her to find a fob to turn it off.

But when she goes downstairs she sees her neighbours are in the street and that the sky has changed from bright blue to "orange and flickering".

"And that's when I started to get really scared," she says.

An accidental fire sparked by farming machinery has spread across fields, railway tracks, Stourbridge golf course and is now in people's gardens.

Farmers have tried to douse the flames and create fire breaks, but thick, black smoke is filling the air and closing in on homes.

Mobile phone footage shared with the BBC shows motorists stranded in the street, watching in horror.

In one, a tearful mum inside a car can be heard telling police her children are at a house in Covert Lane, near the rapidly advancing wildfire.

Holly is frozen in panic as clumps of ash rain from an apocalyptic sky.

"I was too scared to go outside because at that point you couldn't see the street. It was all just fog and smoke and ash," she says.

A three-hour drive away, her mum Anna collapses when she realises the danger her child is in.

Frantic, she sends relatives to take Holly to safety and instructs the hysterical teenager to get dressed, grab their dogs and pet tortoise and get out.

A police officer escorts them away and tells her not to look back, but she cannot help it.

Seven fire engines are dispatched to Stourbridge, where a major incident is declared as commanders realise the scale of the chaos.

Significant wildfires are also raging in parts of south Birmingham and near homes in Stoke-on-Trent, so many appliances are committed elsewhere.

When the major incident is declared, it is taking the fire service 43 minutes to attend a single call. The aim is usually five.

When he arrives on Holly's street, Bournbrook Blue Watch commander Paul Bayliss sees a scene he has never witnessed in his 24-year career.

"It was almost like a tsunami of fire and smoke coming at us."

Sebastian Chauhan, 21, has been a firefighter for a year. He says hardened colleagues fell silent as they surveyed the scene.

"Their faces just go to kind of stone and [I was] thinking, 'OK, it's really kicking off now'," he says.

Desperate residents plead with the crew to save their house first.

"[I've] never had so many people wave at me and look to me for help."

The horizon is a wall of flames and embers the size of tennis balls are falling to the ground.

"It was like it was alive, moving by itself," Chauhan says of the fire.

Poor water pressure means the crew has to siphon water from the swimming pools of several properties in this affluent part of town.

Several firefighters keel over with heat exhaustion, including watch commander Bayliss, but they have to keep going.

"I just knew I had to get up because there was no-one else coming to help at that time," he says.

Bayliss asks for 10 fire engines, only to be told there are not enough available.

For 90 minutes, his team of five and another from Ladywood in Birmingham have to fight the impossible alone until two more crews can get there.

"There was one point where we had one appliance left," call handler Nightingale says.

"We didn't have the fire engines for the crews that needed them desperately at scene. And we didn't have them for the fresh calls either."

Distressed people are shouting down the phone at operators to get help.

"They're screaming at you at this point because they don't know why you've not come to them."

Loxie Williams, 78, is driving back home in Stourbridge after a morning out with husband Robin when they see the churning smoke.

Police stop them getting any closer and, peering through a gap between houses, they see the field directly behind their garden alight.

They decamp to her daughter's house where later, on the TV news, they see their home of 26 years burning down.

"It was a total inferno," she says. "It just couldn't connect. It was such a shock. I was aghast."

Just over 20 miles away in Warstock, Birmingham, a wildfire is ripping through more homes.

Leonie Cotterill yells at her terrified children, aged seven and nine, to get out, but they try to run back inside as they are pulled away.

"[My son's] scream will never leave me," she says.

Their house of 30 years is one of six on the street destroyed, along with multiple gardens.

Chauhan's crew helps to save nine homes in Stourbridge, but 19 are lost across five streets and 18 are damaged.

The entire incident spans an area of about two miles and, eventually, more than 100 firefighters and 30 fire engines battle to contain it.

"If we weren't there, it could have been worse," Chauhan says.

Fires have also destroyed homes in other parts of Birmingham, Willenhall, Stoke-on-Trent and Pershore in Worcestershire, bringing the total to 38.

"It was an extraordinary day and completely unprecedented," says West Midlands chief fire officer Simon Tuhill, who was on the scene in Stourbridge.

"Standing in that road and trying to help colleagues as they made really difficult decisions, prioritise, making sure as many houses were evacuated and looking after as many residents as possible, the enormity of it hit me.

"It's been quite hard to process just how difficult it was."

Tuhill, who has since called for more specialist resources to fight wildfires, such as 4x4 vehicles and aerial firefighting capability, has welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham's pledge to hold a wildfire summit to discuss equipment and resources.

Burnham has promised to be "better prepared next time" and reiterated the summit will be held in the coming weeks.

"We shouldn't live through another summer like the one that we just have," Burnham says.

Dr Kerryn Little, a pyrogeography researcher at the University of Birmingham, researches how wildfires start and spread.

She says the fires came at a time when the landscape was "primed to burn" as a result of the changing climate and "any spark was going to lead to a wildfire".

"I believe that the UK is decades behind other countries in the world, it's really been quite shocking," Little says.

"I think the one good thing about this year is that people are becoming more aware, particularly at a government level, where we really need investment in wildfire preparedness."

Holly and Anna have a very lucky escape. Their house survives almost unscathed, while three neighbouring ones are gutted.

When the teenager returns home, the street appears "dystopian", she says, and she feels incredibly guilty.

"Why is our home here and theirs is all gone? It's just, it's devastating."

She says she no longer opens her curtains.

"I have a view of the whole garden from my window and it's really strange, just like seeing everything so different after 10 years of it always being the same."

When Nightingale finishes her shift and sees photos of the wreckage across Stourbridge, she feels "almost slightly responsible".

"It's definitely the worst day that any of us have experienced, 100%," she adds.

"Ultimately, we're just very grateful that the situation didn't turn out in a death and we're just very, very grateful to the crews for what they did to prevent that."

articles.title: Online grooming becoming 'quicker and easier', police warn
articles.summary: Online grooming is rising, with children as young as five targeted, prompting calls for reform.
articles.body:
Experts are urging parents to talk to their children amid warnings online grooming is becoming "quicker" and "easier" than ever before.

Childline said Snapchat, TikTok and Instagram were the top platforms children named in counselling about online sexual abuse last year. The companies have been approached for comment.

Avon and Somerset Police's child exploitation prevention officer Andri Nicolau said children as young as five can be targeted through social media, gaming and messaging platforms. She urged parents to encourage them to ask for help without fear of blame or punishment.

The warning comes after three men were jailed for grooming a 17-year-old girl on Snapchat before raping her.

Research by the NSPCC found sexual communication offences involving children in the South West have more than doubled since the offence was introduced seven years ago, to 756 in 2024/25.

Of those, 300 were recorded by Avon and Somerset Police, 96 by Gloucestershire Constabulary and 61 by Wiltshire Police.

The charity also said Snapchat was mentioned in 324 counselling sessions about online sexual abuse between April 2025 and March 2026, a 19% increase on the previous year.

TikTok (234) and Instagram (197) were the next most frequently mentioned platforms.

Chris Sherwood, chief executive of the NSPCC, said: "It's deeply disturbing that hundreds of children have come to us in the past year alone, disclosing experiences of online sexual abuse linked to these popular apps and platforms.

"These crimes are highly distressing for victims, often leaving children and their families to deal with devastating lifelong impacts."

Another recent example involved Suleman Aqeel, from Speedwell in Bristol, who was jailed for 17 years at Bristol Crown Court on 30 September.

Aqeel used social media, including Snapchat, to arrange to meet young girls. He also filmed some of his offences and threatened to share intimate videos and images.

New data suggests that this particular form of exploitation of children, known as 'sextortion', has also reached record levels.

The Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) said there has been a sharp rise in the number of young people contacting its confidential Report Remove helpline because they fear sexual images of themselves have been shared, or could be shared, online.

Criminals try to extort or blackmail their victims by threatening to publish the images, which have often been taken by the child themselves.

Nicolau said children spending more time online meant they were increasingly vulnerable to grooming, which is "easier" and "quicker" than ever before.

"With online gaming and social media, you have kids from five years old online, some of them have their own phones, so it can be any age," she said.

She works with schools to inform children how to be safe online, but said they are often unaware of the risks, including not viewing people they meet online as strangers and expecting them to be "nasty" from the start.

Nicolau encouraged any child or young person who believes they are being groomed to "find someone they are comfortable with and speak to them".

She said the police might not be the first choice, but speaking to somebody they trust is what mattered.

Nicolau urged parents to talk to their children and not take away devices or ban them from platforms, warning this could make them feel they were to blame.

"Sit down with your child, tell them it's not their fault, even if they've sent indecent images of themselves," she said.

"Believe them and give them the authorisation to say whatever they need to say."

Ella Bradshaw, the NSPCC's policy and public affairs officer, advised parents to start conversations about online safety as early as possible so that children know that they have a "safe adult" to go to.

"Often, particularly if it's to do with grooming or any kind of sexual or romantic relationship, children can be really scared of being judged and embarrassed to talk," said Bradshaw.

"Making sure that your child knows that you will stand by them, that you will respond with warmth and care rather than judging them or blaming them for what's going on is really important."

James Simmons-Read, who leads the Children's Society national exploitation prevention programme, said there are "huge concerns" about the growing scale of child sexual abuse and exploitation online.

"Perpetrators are always adapting ways they can better reach young people, whether that's through gaming or social media," he said.

He said another worrying trend was young people turning to AI rather than adults for advice and support about online harms.

Simmons-Read urged parents to normalise conversations with young people about their online lives.

Ellen Roome, from Cheltenham, who has been campaigning for improvements to online safety since the death of her son Jools in 2022, said not enough is being done to protect young people on social media.

"Children are regularly being fed content that is either violent or grooming material and I think as it stands, there isn't any platform that is fully safe for them," she said.

"I do think that the social media ban for children will help, but they need to make sure that it is enforced and social media companies are held to account."

Simmons-Read said the social media ban for under 16s , which is due to come into force in 2027, "doesn't go far enough", could be bypassed by criminals and could even discourage young people from speaking up about online grooming.

"We want tech platforms to invest more in detecting exploitation when it's happening on their platforms," he said.

A government spokesperson said it was preparing legislation to make it impossible for children to take, share or view nude images on their devices, which would make the UK the first country to do so.

"Alongside this, tech companies must be part of the solution and meet their legal and moral obligations. Where they fall short, the government will not hesitate to step in," the spokesperson said.

Kerry Smith, chief executive of the IWF, said: "We welcome the commitment to introducing nudity blocking technology on children's devices – but there really is no time to lose."

Meta, which owns Instagram and Facebook, said it is working to "fight and prevent grooming in a range of ways".

A Meta spokesperson said: "This includes restricting contact between adults and teens they're not connected to, and using technology to find and remove known child exploitation imagery.

"We also use behavioural signals to identify accounts showing possible signs of grooming or a sexual interest in children.

"Based on the strength of the signals, we either prevent them from finding and following teens or we remove their account completely."

Snapchat and TikTok have all been approached by the BBC for comment.

articles.title: Stratford teen's death inspires mum's drive for earlier rare cancer diagnosis
articles.summary: Hannah York hopes new guidance will help doctors spot signs of soft tissue sarcomas sooner.
articles.body:
Liberty York was 19 when she died from a rare form of cancer, two days after her birthday.

A year after her death, her mother Hannah York has talked about her strength and the parts of her daughter that existed outside of her illness.

"The first thing that comes to mind when I think about Liberty is how kind she was and thoughtful," she said.

To Hannah, she was still the same determined teenager throughout the final year of her life, before she died from an angiosarcoma, a rare form of soft tissue sarcoma, a type of cancer which starts in areas of the body such as muscle and fat.

The first signs appeared in May 2024 when Liberty, from Stratford-upon-Avon, Warwickshire, began feeling unusually tired and nauseous.

A year earlier she had been diagnosed with Addison's disease, a rare autoimmune condition, so at first the family thought it was possible the two could be linked.

Liberty was referred to see a specialist but while the family waited for answers, she developed swelling and pain in her left breast.

"We went to see the GP about the swelling and she thought it was mastitis because it was red as well and painful.," Hannah said.

"The [cancer's] main symptom is the swelling or change in skin. Liberty's swelling kept getting bigger and bigger."

Antibiotics were prescribed but they failed to work and doctors initially thought she had an abscess.

Later, Hannah said, attention turned towards the possibility that hormones could be responsible.

"Liberty was on a teenage cancer ward and they said it was very common," she said.

"So many teenagers, it's put down to hormones and unfortunately they said they see it every day."

The swelling that had begun as a small area of concern just weeks earlier had become a tumour weighing 10lb (4.5kg) by the time surgery took place.

For Hannah, that moment brought relief that they finally had an answer, but also the harsh reality of what her daughter was facing.

"Liberty's type of sarcoma was a particularly aggressive sarcoma and, after she was operated on, it had spread to her lungs in just six weeks," she remembered.

"The difference between days and weeks to diagnosis is so important with sarcoma. She didn't get a fighting chance."

Liberty died in the early hours of 1 June 2025, two days after celebrating her 19th birthday.

In the months since, Hannah said she had tried to channel her grief into raising awareness of the disease that took her daughter.

She is supporting the Child Cancer Smart campaign, led by CCLG: The Children & Young People's Cancer Association, as it launches new guidelines for healthcare professionals, aimed at improving recognition of soft tissue sarcomas in children and young people.

These cancers account for about 7% of childhood cancers, according to the charity, but experts say diagnosis can often be delayed because symptoms resemble more common conditions.

"Liberty was an incredibly strong person with a very strong sense of right and wrong. She was very opinionated, which I loved about her," Hannah said.

"I don't know if any earlier diagnosis could have saved her, but she'd have had more of a chance.

"Her cancer was rare, underfunded and under-researched, so the best chance of helping other people is by making sure they are diagnosed early."

articles.title: Four killed as Indonesia battles worst forest fires in more than a decade
articles.summary: The deaths come as Jakarta says it will accept foreign help to tackle its worst forest fires in more than a decade.
articles.body:
Four people tackling a wildfire in a national park on Indonesia’s island of Java have been killed, the Forestry Ministry said, as the country battles its worst forest fires in more than a decade.

The victims were caught in the flames on Thursday in Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in East Java , the ministry said on Friday.

Two others suffered serious burns and are receiving medical treatment. The forest fires have extended beyond Indonesia’s borders, blanketing neighbouring countries in haze, Reuters reported.

The ministry did not identify the victims. In a statement, it expressed “deep condolences” and paid tribute to the “courage and dedication” of the officers, volunteers and residents working on the fire lines.

The deaths, it said, were “a reminder that extinguishing forest and land fires is a high-risk operation”, adding that safety “must be the main concern”, including tracking how the fire is spreading and the wind direction, keeping evacuation routes ready and assessing conditions before and during operations.

The islands of Sumatra and Borneo, close to Singapore and Malaysia, are the worst affected.

The ministry said satellite monitoring detected 799 high-confidence hotspots nationwide as of Thursday night, up 427 from the day before. The ministry cautioned that hotspots are not the same as fires, as one blaze can register as several.

Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has approved accepting help from neighbouring countries, Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said, according to Reuters.

Malaysia offered last month to send three helicopters, an aircraft and 52 personnel, but there has been no follow-up, Reuters reported. Singapore has also said it is ready to help.

Indonesia has faced heavy criticism over the fires, which have caused respiratory problems for hundreds of thousands of people and forced school closures in Malaysia and East Timor, according to Reuters.

articles.title: Cumbrian charity fears closure could leave mums suicidal
articles.summary: The Happy Mums Foundation supports women experiencing postpartum mental health challenges.
articles.body:
A charity has said it is "terrified" new mums suffering from suicidal thoughts will be left with nowhere to turn if its group sessions end due to funding pressures.

The Happy Mums Foundation, which supports women experiencing postpartum mental health challenges, was set up in 2015 and has helped more than 1,000 families across Cumbria.

Charity director Lucinda Bray fears the loss of the in-person "safe place" could worsen the mental health of vulnerable women in the county.

Women who have attended the sessions say the charity, which would move online only, offers "no judgement" peer support and helps mums feel less isolated when experiencing trauma.

Bray said: "I'm terrified, if we don't have in-person groups for mums, where will they go? What will they do?

"Being able to talk about suicidal thinking, is actually quite a good preventative factor, if that doesn't have an outlet and you don't have a safe space to talk about those things, where might they go?"

First-time mum Amy described motherhood as "absolutely wonderful" but admitted it could be stressful and overwhelming at times.

"The long nights, the crying and not knowing what it is they want, you've just been handed a tiny human being and you're meant to just know what to do and having the expectations of mum knows best.

"I didn't have a clue and I think a lot of mums are in the same boat."

At first Amy found it difficult to leave the house with her daughter who was born prematurely.

Now, she attends the charity's teen to 25 group, which has helped her build confidence.

"Obviously everyone absolutely adores the babies here but it's called Happy Mums for a reason," she said.

"There's plenty of support out there for babies, but it's nice to have something that is more about the mums."

Amy said without the support of the group she would struggle more to get out and about.

"When I'm feeling low with my depression or anxiety and more anxious about going out I know that I can come to Happy Mums, I look forward to it," she said.

"Without it I'd struggle more with speaking to people and asking for the help."

The Happy Mums Foundation had previously received funding from Comic Relief, The National Lottery, The Cumbria Foundation and the NHS.

The group says over the last year funding for preventative mental health services has become increasingly difficult to secure.

Bray said the 13 weekly support groups have already been reduced to five, and without investment the charity will be forced to move groups online or close completely.

Growing financial pressures across the charities sector has been evident in recent months, including the closure of suicide prevention charity Papyrus in September.

National Council for Voluntary Organisations' chief influencing officer Leigh Brimicombe said the current financial climate was "tough" for charity organisations.

He said the cost of living crisis meant there was a "growing need for support in communities but also less money available for donors or funders to give, compounded by increased running costs for charities themselves".

Labour MP for Penrith and Solway, Markus Campbell-Savours, sent a letter of concern about the future of foundation to the Cumbria, Northumberland, Tyne and Wear NHS Trust.

In reply, chief executive James Duncan said "peer-led and community-based support can form a valuable part of the wider network for support available to women and families".

He added although formal joint working with the NHS was not possible due to the distinction between peer-led and clinical services, the potential closure was "particularly concerning given the relatively limited number of voluntary and community sector organisations providing this type of support across Cumbria".

The Department of Health and Social Care has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Meta releases Muse Spark Open AI model with 816 billion parameters; runs on two Apple Mac Studios
articles.summary: Meta has released Muse Spark Open, an open-weight artificial intelligence (AI) model designed for coding, complex reasoning and tasks that require
articles.body: Meta has released Muse Spark Open, an open-weight artificial intelligence (AI) model designed for coding, complex reasoning and tasks that require multiple steps. The company says the model can run on a desktop setup using two Apple Mac Studios powered by M5 Ultra chips, making it possible to use an advanced AI model locally rather than relying only on cloud services. As stated by the company in its official announcement, Muse Spark Open has 816 billion total parameters, with 42 billion active parameters, and supports a context window of 1 million tokens. Developers can access the model through several AI platforms or download its weights to customize it for their needs.Meta Muse Spark Open: Features and capabilitiesMeta said Muse Spark Open is designed for long-running tasks, complex software development and agentic AI workflows, in which a model can carry out multiple steps towards a goal.The model is natively multimodal, meaning it can work with different types of information. It has 816 billion total parameters, of which 42 billion are active, and a context window of 1 million tokens. A large context window allows a model to process a substantial amount of information in a single interaction.Meta said it tested the model on tasks involving software development and video editing. In one test, the model was used to make bug fixes and add features to Ice Cubes, an open-source Mastodon client, before building the application. In another, it worked with DaVinci Resolve to review video footage frame by frame, identify suitable moments and crop clips into a vertical format.The company also said the model includes optimised GPU kernels that deliver kernel-level speed improvements of 1.03 to 3.95 times on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. Meta reported a 3% overall speed improvement on AMD MI350.How to access Muse Spark Open AI modelMeta says Muse Spark Open is available through AI inference platforms including Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. Developers can download its model weights through Hugging Face, Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden and Microsoft Foundry Models. The model supports inference engines such as SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, Apple MLX, llama.cpp and Unsloth. Developers can also customise it using PyTorch.For local use, Meta has optimised Muse Spark Open for Apple's M5 Ultra Mac Studio through the MLX framework. According to the company, two Mac Studios can work together to provide enough unified memory to hold the model.Meta said it has added safety training to the open-weight version and evaluated it under its Superintelligence Scaling Framework. The company said the model met the safety thresholds required for release.The model is being released under the Muse Model License, which allows many developers to use it for free but includes limited commercial terms. articles.summary: A father from Milton Keynes has spent more than £80,000 transforming his back garden into an 80-square-metre tropical hideout complete with an 8,000-litre
articles.body: A father from Milton Keynes has spent more than £80,000 transforming his back garden into an 80-square-metre tropical hideout complete with an 8,000-litre fish tank, 14 Koi fish, 15 Madagascan day geckos, palm trees and a beer tap. Andy Corrie, 41, built the space himself as a personal retreat where he could relax after work and spend time away from his busy routine.According to The Metro UK, the project initially surprised his wife, Sarah, and their neighbours, who were not convinced by his plans. However, the space helped them understand his vision. Corrie began planning the project about three years before June 2022 and continued adding new features. His family also enjoys the garden retreat, which he hopes to expand further.How did Andy Corrie turn his back garden into an £80,000 tropical hideoutCorrie transformed his Milton Keynes home's garden into what he calls his ‘man cave’. The 80-square-metre space was built single-handedly and designed to provide an escape from everyday life. As a construction worker, Corrie deals with building plans each day, which helped him approach the project.Corrie said, “My wife, Sarah thought I was absolutely crazy at first, but now it’s built she understands where I was coming from when I was trying to explain the plan”.“I started working on the plans about three years ago and I’m still adding to it – any new idea I have, I just throw it in”.What makes Andy Corrie’s £80,000 garden hideout a tropical paradiseThe hideout combines tropical greenery, an aquarium, and entertainment features within the garden space. Its main attraction is an 8,000-litre fish tank containing 14 Koi fish. The retreat also houses 15 Madagascan day geckos and features palm trees, a sound system and a beer tap.Corrie spent part of the £80,000 budget on the tropical plants, which grow from large underground planters. He described the setting as an unusual place, with palm trees that appear to grow straight out of the ground. The combination of plants, fish and other features gives the garden its tropical character.How Andy Corrie maintains his tropical hideout with Koi fish and Madagascan day geckosMaintaining the tropical environment involves keeping the fish tank at a constant temperature of 24 degrees. Corrie bought his 14 Koi fish from dealerships across the UK, with some costing as much as £10,000. After the aquarium was established, someone suggested introducing lizards because they enjoy the warm climate.Corrie followed the suggestion and added 15 Madagascan day geckos to the space. His children also enjoy spending time around the fish. His four-year-old daughter, Evie, helps him feed the Koi fish every day, while his one-year-old son, Archie, enjoys coming into the hideout and attacking the plants.Andy Corrie plans to add a pool table and more tropical animals to his garden hideoutDespite spending more than £80,000 on the garden project, Corrie has not finished developing the space. He wants to extend the hideout to accommodate a pool table and has considered introducing more tropical animals.His ideas include tree frogs and possibly monkeys, with the aim of making the garden feel even more like a jungle. The plans reflect his approach since he first began working on it. Corrie said he continued to add features whenever he came up with a new idea.The hideout also gives him somewhere to unwind after a hard day's work and relax at weekends without travelling far from home. articles.title: Alone in Gaza: Genocide leaves Palestinian man without family or a home
articles.summary: One man wanders Gaza in search of somewhere to sleep, having lost his family in an Israeli strike.
articles.body:
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Every morning, Mahmoud Khalla goes to the nearby cemetery to visit the graves of the family members he lost during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

He has held on to this morning routine in the months since he buried them, imagining his family is still around.

For Mahmoud, 40, the cemetery is the resting place of some of the people he has loved the most in his life.

His wife, his three children, his parents, his two brothers and their families, his sister and her children, and other relatives had all gathered in their family home in Jabalia, northern Gaza, on December 21, 2023.

An Israeli strike then targeted the five-storey family home, destroying the building and killing all 39 people inside. Mahmoud left his home shortly before it hit and is the only one left in his family.

Mahmoud remembers that day with heartache. Israeli tanks had surrounded the area near the house in Jabalia, northern Gaza, making it dangerous for people to move around. Food was already scarce due to the ongoing Israeli siege. In the evening, Mahmoud left the house in search of provisions to feed his family.

“I told them I would go and see what was available,” he told Al Jazeera. “As soon as I had been out for about 15 minutes, I heard a huge explosion.”

“I ran back and discovered that the targeted house was ours. I was in complete shock. But I pulled myself together. With the help of a few neighbours who were still in the area, we tried to rescue anyone who might be under the rubble.”

Israeli air attacks, quadcopters and surveillance aircraft continued to target the area. It made it impossible for Mahmoud and his neighbours to search for survivors.

“A surveillance aircraft dropped a bomb on us, so we immediately ran away,” he says. “We came back the next morning.”

Ambulances and civil defence teams were also unable to reach the site that night.

With this sense of helplessness, he imagined that some of his family might still be alive under the rubble, waiting to be rescued. He felt as though he had died a thousand times that night.

The following morning, he returned to the site and called out to his family members who might be beneath the ruined home. Nobody answered, and it was at this moment he realised he had lost nearly every person he loved.

“There were five floors of rubble. It was impossible for us to pull anyone out,” he said.

That attack marked the beginning of a long period of emptiness for Mahmoud. With his home destroyed and almost all of his relatives killed or displaced to the south, he had nowhere to go.

“Even my uncles had been killed,” he says. “Their house, opposite ours, was targeted nine days before our family home. Eighteen people were killed in that attack. The rest of the family had gone south.”

Mahmoud spent the following months displaced and alone. He moved between the streets in search of somewhere to sleep for the night. It was difficult to find shelter among displaced families when he had no relation to them.

“I was sleeping in the streets, or in cars or vehicles whenever I found one that was open,” he says. “I was totally lonely and homeless.”

With no shelter at all, Mahmoud was vulnerable to Israeli attacks. The struggle for food became as urgent as the need to find somewhere safe to sleep.

“You don’t know whether a bullet will hit you, whether a rocket will come, whether you will find food or where you will sleep,” he said.

After a “ceasefire” was announced for Gaza in October 2025, families began the difficult search for their missing loved ones. Nearly a year later, an estimated 8,000 people remain missing, their bodies likely under the rubble of their homes or in other locations.

Months after the “ceasefire” began and bombing decreased, Mahmoud started recovering the remains of his family members himself. They had been entombed among the remains of their home for the last 29 months.

“The feeling that my family was still under the rubble, without being buried, was very difficult,” he says. “It never left me.”

He approached the civil defence, the Red Cross and other authorities for help. But he says a severe shortage of equipment and a huge number of other families requesting assistance meant they could be of little help.

Eventually, with the help of friends and neighbours who volunteered to work alongside him, he began the heartbreaking task of recovering his loved ones himself by hand.

He began recovering the remains around May this year, in a process that took three months.

“Sometimes, we managed to recover one person in a day. Sometimes, it took two days,” he said.

The first people he found were two relatives who had been sheltering with the family. The last were his sister and her children, who had been buried together.

He buried his family members at a cemetery near Jabalia an-Nazla, in northern Gaza.

“I felt a great sense of relief when I finally buried them,” he said. “It took me three months to recover all of their remains, working day by day.”

articles.title: In 2012, Jack Dorsey paid $9.99 million for a San Francisco Sea Cliff home and began rebuilding within months; nearly 14 years later, he owns the house next door too, with the two properties costing $31.9 million
articles.summary: For most homebuyers, buying a house means years of saving and planning a future.
articles.body: For most homebuyers, buying a house means years of saving and planning a future. For Jack Dorsey, Twitter’s co-founder, buying a multimillion-dollar home overlooking the Pacific Ocean was apparently only the beginning of a project.Back in February 2012, Dorsey paid a whopping $9.99 million for a modern home in Sea Cliff, one of San Francisco’s most exclusive neighbourhoods. After buying the house, renovation work started. Now almost 14 years later, the project has evolved into an elaborate residential redevelopment, and Dorsey has added the neighbouring property to his real estate portfolio.From a $9.99 million home to a $31.9 million property portfolioThe combined purchase price of the two properties stands at approximately $31.9 million. Yet, as a report published by the New York Post on October 13, 2026, highlights, the renovation continues to attract attention for its extraordinary duration and the construction activity.Dorsey bought the first property at 830 El Camino del Mar through a limited liability company in February 2012. As per reports, the modernist residence was built in 1965 and originally had two bedrooms and two bathrooms. It is spread across 0.59 acre and measures around 3,734 square feet.Location, the heroThe location was the main hero. Sea Cliff offers stunning views of the Pacific Ocean, China Beach and the Golden Gate Bridge. It is San Francisco’s most sought-after residential region for a reason. From winding streets and greenery to large private homes, everything here looks dreamy and has a character.A long-term redevelopment projectHowever, the property became a long-term redevelopment project rather than a home. In December 2013, a major redevelopment application proposed improvements worth approximately $3.7 million.The plans included:Seismic strengtheningAdditional living spaceRoof decksA planted roofHe got the permit for redevelopment in June 2017, nearly three and a half years after the application was filed.In 2020, another major redesign followed which included changes to the windows, courtyard, rooms and exterior finishes. Approval arrived in July 2022, but further applications continued to cover different aspects of the project.Second addition to Dorsey’s real estateThe second major addition to Dorsey’s real estate holdings came in November 2018. He purchased the neighbouring residence at 840 El Camino del Mar for $21.9 million which was built in 1962. It was a five-bedroom, three-bathroom property spread across 0.62 acre.With this purchase, Dorsey’s combined expenditure on the two properties reached about $31.9 million (excluding renovation expenses). Together, the properties occupy approximately 1.21 acres.What does the billionaire’s coastal home look like?The plans for Dorsey’s original property suggest a retreat designed around privacy, nature and wellness rather than conventional displays of luxury.The home is supposed to incorporate stonework, reclaimed redwood siding, expansive windows and three vegetation-covered roofs. There’s also a courtyard at the centre of the design, while the ocean-facing spaces make the most of the property's coastal setting.The proposed amenities are:Sauna complexSteam roomCold plunge poolA hot tub adjoining the primary bedroom, overlooking the oceanA gymA fire pitSustainability and infrastructureThe plans also include 34 solar panels, while separate applications have addressed an underground water-storage tank, retaining walls, landscaping and other building systems. The fire-protection plans call for 122 sprinklers and a dedicated 145-foot water line.The timeline raises a question. In Dorsey’s case, the answer lies in permit applications and revisions rather than one uninterrupted construction project. Also San Francisco’s coastal setting and established residential neighbourhoods provide a challenging backdrop for large-scale construction.For the moment, the story of his Sea Cliff property remains one of an exceptionally expensive home undergoing an exceptionally prolonged transformation. And in Sea Cliff, where ocean views and multimillion-dollar houses are part of the appeal, even a billionaire’s dream home has to contend with building permits and construction schedules.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: She once worked as a labourer on other people's farms; today Chhabita Pramanik leads 347 self-help groups, supports 500 families and helped build a network of nearly 3,500 women
articles.summary: Chhabita Pramanik once worked as a labourer on other people’s farms in Bankura, West Bengal.
articles.body: Chhabita Pramanik once worked as a labourer on other people’s farms in Bankura, West Bengal. Today, she cultivates her own land, earns a monthly net income of around ₹15,000 from agriculture and related activities, and leads a network of 347 self-help groups (SHGs) supporting nearly 500 rural families. Her work has helped bring together almost 3,500 women through farming, food processing and collective businesses.According to the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), Pramanik’s journey began with just two acres of land. She gradually developed her farm by adopting scientific farming methods and resource-saving practices. Her association with Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK), Bankura, under the West Bengal Comprehensive Area Development Corporation (WBCADC), helped her gain technical knowledge and learn how to turn agricultural work into a more sustainable source of income. But her work soon extended beyond her own farm. Pramanik began organising women in her village, helping them work together and explore ways to earn independently.Started a group with just 10 womenPramanik began her leadership journey by forming Rangamatichar Vachati Swanirvar Dal, a self-help group with only 10 women members. According to ICAR, the initiative later developed into Dihipara Monalisa Sangha, which initially connected around 500 women and eventually grew into a collective involving nearly 3,500 women across the district. As reported by Anandabazar Patrika, she faced resistance when she began organising women around 25 years ago. Some influential local people objected to women working outside their homes and taking loans. The report says Pramanik was socially isolated, and people sometimes shut their doors when she approached them.She wanted women to move away from borrowing from moneylenders who charged interest of 5% per month, according to the report. She explained the value of working together, saying, “I had explained to them that if women worked together, we could get out of that cycle.” Her efforts gradually changed attitudes in the village. The women who were once discouraged from stepping outside their homes are now involved in farming and group enterprises, with some men also helping them with their work.How scientific farming changed the workPramanik and members of her self-help group approached KVK Bankura for technical support and demonstrations. With guidance from KVK scientists, they introduced resource-conserving methods for paddy cultivation in the locality. According to ICAR, these methods improved productivity and helped farmers use resources more efficiently than conventional practices. She also received training in oilseed farming, integrated nutrient management and groundnut oil processing. The women’s collective learnt vermicompost production, mushroom cultivation, growing vegetables outside the usual season under shade-net structures, and processing agricultural produce into higher-value products.Under the Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY), KVK Bankura helped establish a mushroom spawn production unit, a shade-net facility and an electric ‘dheki’ for processing brown rice. These facilities gave the women opportunities to earn from processing and value addition rather than depending only on the sale of raw crops. According to ICAR, brown rice produced by Pramanik and her collective is now sold through a retail outlet run by the West Bengal government. The group has also been involved in awareness campaigns promoting the balanced use of fertilisers.From growing crops to building group businessesThe women associated with Pramanik’s network grow paddy, vegetables, groundnuts, potatoes, turmeric, mustard and other crops. Some of their processed products, including rice and spices, are marketed through organisations that help connect them with buyers. Their markets have expanded beyond Bankura to Durgapur and surrounding areas, with products also reaching customers outside the region.Pramanik continues to work on the farm herself. As reported by Anandbazar Patrika, she still harvests paddy, plants vegetables and processes rice while also managing the accounts of the women’s collective. She has learnt basic computer skills and can maintain records and enter names on a computer. In an interview with Anandabazar Patrika, she described the collective effort behind the work: “This life is not mine alone. It is ours.”The group’s work has also reached beyond farming. Women from the collective gradually took charge of organising the village’s Durga Puja celebrations, including managing the committee and meeting expenses. It has become another example of women taking on responsibilities in community life.Supports 500 families as a community resource personPramanik currently serves as a Senior Community Resource Person (CRP), a role through which she supports nearly 500 rural families. ICAR says she leads 347 self-help groups across Bankura district, helping women adopt sustainable farming methods and take part in collective enterprises. Her work has received recognition from government and agricultural institutions. According to ICAR, she was recently felicitated by the Governor of West Bengal for her contribution to rural development.From working on other people’s farms to cultivating her own land and helping thousands of women work together, Pramanik’s journey has been shaped by farming knowledge and collective organisation.
